{{Short description|Function defined on integers in number theory}}
In [[number theory]], the '''Lagarias arithmetic derivative''' or '''number derivative''' is a [[function (mathematics)|function]] defined for [[integer]]s, based on [[prime factorization]], by analogy with the [[product rule]] for the [[derivative|derivative of a function]] that is used in [[mathematical analysis]].

There are many versions of "arithmetic derivatives", including the one discussed in this article (the Lagarias arithmetic derivative), such as Ihara's arithmetic derivative and Buium's arithmetic derivatives.

==Early history==
The arithmetic derivative was introduced by Spanish mathematician Josè Mingot Shelly in 1911.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Shelly |first1=D. J. M. |title=Una cuestión de la teoria de los numeros |journal=Association Esp. Granada |date=1911 |pages=1–12 |jfm=42.0209.02 |url=https://zbmath.org/?q=an:42.0209.02}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Lava |first1=Paolo Pietro |last2=Balzarotti |first2=Giorgio |title=La derivata aritmetica: Alla scoperta di un nuovo approccio alla teoria dei numeri}}</ref> The arithmetic derivative also appeared in the 1950 [[William Lowell Putnam Competition|Putnam Competition]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Scholes |first1=John |title=10th Putnam 1950 |url=https://prase.cz/kalva/putnam/putn50.html}}</ref>

==Definition==
For [[natural number]]s {{mvar|n}}, the arithmetic derivative {{math|''D''(''n'')}}<ref group=note name="notation">In this article we use [[Oliver Heaviside]]'s notation {{math|''D''(''n'')}} for the arithmetic derivative of {{mvar|n}}. There are various other notations possible, such as {{math|''n''′}}; a full discussion is available [[Differential operator#Notations|here]] for general [[differential operator]]s, of which the arithmetic derivative can be considered one. Heaviside's notation is used here because it highlights the fact that the arithmetic derivative is a [[Arithmetic function|function over the integers]] and yields itself better notation-wise to [[function iteration]] {{math|''D''<sup>&hairsp;''k''</sup>}} for second and higher-order arithmetic derivatives.</ref> is defined as follows:

* {{math|1=''D''(''p'')  =  1}} for any [[prime number|prime]] {{mvar|p}}.
* {{math|1=''D''(''mn'')  =  ''D''(''m'')''n'' + ''mD''(''n'')}} for any <math>m, n \in \N</math> ([[product rule|Leibniz rule]]).

==Extensions beyond natural numbers==

[[Edward Barbeau|Edward J. Barbeau]] extended the [[domain of a function|domain]] to all integers by showing that the choice {{math|1=''D''(−''n'') = −''D''(''n'')}} uniquely extends the domain to the integers and is consistent with the product formula. Barbeau also further extended it to the [[rational number]]s, showing that the familiar [[quotient rule]] gives a well-defined derivative on <math>\Q</math>:

<math display="block">D\!\left(\frac{m}{n}\right) = \frac{D(m)n-m D(n)}{n^2} .</math><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Barbeau |first1=Edward |title=Remarks on an Arithmetic Derivative |journal=[[Canadian Mathematical Bulletin]] |year=1961 |volume=4 |issue=2 |page=117-122 |doi=10.4153/CMB-1961-013-0|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Barbeau |first1=Edward |title=Problem |journal=Canad. Math. Congress Notes |date=April 1973 |volume=5 |issue=8 |page=6-7}}</ref>

[[Victor Ufnarovski]] and [[Bo Åhlander]] expanded it to the [[irrational number|irrationals]] that can be written as the product of primes raised to arbitrary rational powers, allowing expressions like <math>D(\sqrt{3}\,)</math> to be computed.<ref name="jis2003">{{cite journal |last1=Ufnarovski |first1=Victor |last2=Ahlander |first2=Bo |title=How to Differentiate a Number |journal=Journal of Integer Sequences |date=2003 |volume=6 |issue=3 |url=https://cs.uwaterloo.ca/journals/JIS/VOL6/Ufnarovski/ufnarovski.pdf}}</ref>

The arithmetic derivative can also be extended to any [[unique factorization domain]] (UFD),<ref name="jis2003"/> such as the [[Gaussian integer]]s and the [[Eisenstein integer]]s, and its associated [[field of fractions]]. If the UFD is a [[polynomial ring]], then the arithmetic derivative is the same as the [[Derivation (differential algebra)|derivation]] over said polynomial ring. For example, the regular [[derivative]] is the arithmetic derivative for the rings of [[univariate]] [[real number|real]] and [[complex number|complex]] [[polynomial]] and [[rational function]]s, which can be proven using the [[fundamental theorem of algebra]]. 

The arithmetic derivative has also been extended to the [[ring of integers modulo n|ring of integers modulo ''n'']].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Krebs |first1=Mike |last2=Emmons |first2=Caleb |last3=Shaheen |first3=Anthony |title=How to Differentiate an Integer Modulo n |journal=The College Mathematics Journal |date=November 2009 |volume=40 |issue=5 |pages=345–353 |doi=10.4169/074683409X475661 |s2cid=122997343 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.4169/074683409X475661|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Elementary properties==
The Leibniz rule implies that {{math|1=''D''(0) = 0}} (take {{math|1=''m'' = ''n'' = 0}}) and {{math|1=''D''(1) = 0}} (take {{math|1=''m'' = ''n'' = 1}}).

The ''power rule'' is also valid for the arithmetic derivative. For any integers {{mvar|k}} and {{math|''n'' ≥ 0}}:

<math display="block">D(k^n) = nk^{n-1} D(k).</math>

This allows one to compute the derivative from the prime factorization of an integer, <math display="inline">x = \prod\limits_{p \in \mathbb{P}} p^{n_p} </math> (in which <math display="inline">n_p = \nu_p(x)</math> is the [[p-adic valuation|''p''-adic valuation]] of {{mvar|x}}) :

<math display="block">D(x) = \sum\limits_{p \in \mathbb{P}} \frac{x}{p^{n_p}} n_p \,  p^{n_p-1} D(p)
= \sum_{\stackrel{p \vert x}{p \in \mathbb{P}}} n_p \frac x p D(p)
= x \sum_{\stackrel{p \vert x}{p \in \mathbb{P}}} \frac {n_p} {p} D(p).
</math>

This shows that if one knows the derivative for all prime numbers, then  the derivative is fully known. In fact, the family of arithmetic partial derivatives <math display=inline>\frac \partial {\partial p}</math> relative to the prime number <math display=inline>p</math>, defined by <math display=inline>\frac \partial {\partial p}(q)=0</math> for all primes <math display=inline>q</math>, except for <math display=inline>q=p</math> for which <math display=inline>\frac \partial {\partial p}(p)=1</math> allows to write any derivative as an (improper) infinite sum (see below for an example). Note that, for this derivative, we have <math>\frac {\partial x}{\partial p} = n_p \frac x p</math>.

Usually, one takes the derivative such that <math display=inline>D(p)=1</math> for all primes {{mvar|p}}, so that 
<math display="block">D=\sum\limits_{p \in \mathbb{P}}\frac \partial {\partial p} \text{, and } D(x)= x \sum\limits_{p \in \mathbb{P}} \frac {n_p} p.</math>

With this derivative, we have for example: 
<math display="block">D(60) = D(2^2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5) = 60 \cdot \left(\frac{2}{2} + \frac{1}{3} + \frac{1}{5}\right) = 92,</math>
or
<math display="block">D(81) = D(3^4) = 4\cdot 3^3\cdot D(3) = 4\cdot 27\cdot 1 = 108.</math>

And the [[integer sequence|sequence]] of number derivatives for {{math|1=''x'' = 0, 1, 2, …}} begins {{OEIS|id=A003415}}:

<math display="block">0, 0, 1, 1, 4, 1, 5, 1, 12, 6, 7, 1, 16, 1, 9, \ldots</math>

==Related functions==
The ''logarithmic derivative'' <math display="block">\operatorname{ld}(x)=\frac{D(x)}{x} = \sum_{\stackrel{p \,\mid\, x}{p \in \mathbb{P}}} \frac {\nu_p(x)} {p}</math> is a [[totally additive function]]: <math display="block">\operatorname{ld}(x \cdot y) = \operatorname{ld}(x)+\operatorname{ld}(y).</math>

Let <math>p</math> be a prime. The ''arithmetic partial derivative'' of <math>x</math> with respect to <math>p</math> is defined as <math display="inline">D_p(x) = \frac {\nu_p(x)} {p} x.</math> So, the arithmetic derivative of <math>x</math> is given as <math display="inline">D(x) = \sum_{\stackrel{p \,\mid\, x}{p \in \mathbb{P}}} D_p(x).</math>

Let <math>S</math> be a nonempty set of primes. The ''arithmetic subderivative'' of <math>x</math> with respect to <math>S</math> is defined as <math display="inline">D_S(x) = \sum_{\stackrel{p \,\mid\, x}{p \in S}} D_p(x).</math>
If <math>S</math> is the set of all primes, then <math>D_S(x) = D(x),</math> the usual arithmetic derivative. If <math>S=\{p\}</math>, then <math>D_S(x) = D_p(x),</math> the arithmetic partial derivative. 

An arithmetic function <math>f</math> is ''Leibniz-additive'' if there is a [[totally multiplicative function]] <math>h_f</math> such that <math>f(mn) = f(m)h_f(n)+f(n)h_f(m)</math> for all positive integers <math>m</math> and <math>n</math>. A motivation for this concept is the fact that Leibniz-additive functions are generalizations of the arithmetic derivative <math>D</math>; namely, <math>D</math> is Leibniz-additive with <math>h_D(n)=n</math>.

The function <math>\delta</math> given in Section 3.5 of the book by Sandor and Atanassov is, in fact, exactly the same as the usual arithmetic derivative <math>D</math>.

==Inequalities and bounds==
E. J. Barbeau examined bounds on the arithmetic derivative<ref>Barbeau, E.J. (1961). Remarks on an arithmetic derivative. URL: https://www.cambridge.org/core/services/aop-cambridge-core/content/view/1FD7F09AD3972692FC97BB23A21D0BD8/S0008439500050773a.pdf/remarks_on_an_arithmetic_derivative.pdf</ref> and found that
<math display="block">D(n) \leq \frac{n \log_2 n}{2}</math>
and
<math display="block">D(n) \geq \Omega(n)\, n^{\frac{\Omega(n)-1}{\Omega(n)}}</math>
where {{math|Ω(''n'')}}, a [[prime omega function]], is the number of prime factors in {{mvar|n}}. In both bounds above, equality always occurs when {{mvar|n}} is a [[power of 2]].

Dahl, Olsson and Loiko found the arithmetic derivative of natural numbers is bounded by<ref>Dahl, N., Olsson, J., Loiko, A. (2011). Investigations on the properties of the arithmetic derivative. On page 4. URL: https://arxiv.org/pdf/1108.4762.pdf</ref>
<math display="block">D(n) \leq \frac{n \log_p n}{p}</math>
where {{mvar|p}} is the least prime in {{mvar|n}} and equality holds when {{mvar|n}} is a power of {{mvar|p}}.

[[Alexander Loiko]], [[Jonas Ernst Olsson|Jonas Olsson]] and [[Niklas Dahl]] found that it is impossible to find similar bounds for the arithmetic derivative extended to rational numbers by proving that between any two rational numbers there are other rationals with arbitrary large or small derivatives (note that this means that the arithmetic derivative is not a [[continuous function]] from <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> to <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>).

==Order of the average==
We have {{citation needed|date=November 2025}}
<math display="block">\sum_{n \le x} \frac{D(n)}{n} = T_0 x + O(\log x \log\log x)</math>
and
<math display="block">\sum_{n \le x} D(n) = \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)T_0 x^2 + O(x^{1+\delta})</math>

for any ''δ''&nbsp;>&nbsp;0, where 

<math display="block">T_0 = \sum_p \frac{1}{p(p-1)}. </math>

==Relevance to number theory==

[[Victor Ufnarovski]] and [[Bo Åhlander]] have detailed the function's connection to famous number-theoretic [[conjecture]]s like the [[twin prime conjecture]], the prime triples conjecture, and [[Goldbach's conjecture]]. For example, Goldbach's conjecture would imply, for each {{math|''k'' > 1}} the existence of an {{mvar|n}} so that {{math|1=''D''(''n'') = 2''k''}}. The twin prime conjecture would imply that there are infinitely many {{mvar|k}} for which {{math|1=''D''<sup>2</sup>(''k'') = 1}}.<ref name="jis2003"/>
